title: Seeing their side
hookLine: imagining another's view differs from feeling their feelings, and both matter

cards: A friend has just lost her job, and two people sit with her at the kitchen table. One is an old colleague who reads her perfectly: knows what she's afraid of, what to say, what not to say, and stays calm doing it.
The other is her brother, who can barely breathe for worry, who feels every flinch, and who keeps saying the wrong thing. Which one is the empathic one?
The honest answer is that each is doing a different half of the same work. Today pulls those halves apart, so each can be seen clearly.

teach.h: READING A MIND, SHARING A FEELING.
teach.b: First, the two halves. Researchers often separate taking someone's perspective, working out what they think, want and know, from sharing their feelings, being moved by what they feel.
The first is sometimes called cognitive empathy, the second emotional or affective empathy.
Second, they come apart. Research from Tania Singer's group and others suggests the two lean on partly different networks in the brain, and a person can be strong in one and weaker in the other.
A sharp negotiator can read the room without being moved by anyone in it. A tender heart can be flooded with someone's pain and still misunderstand what they need.
Third, each needs the other. Feeling without understanding can turn into distress, the drowning from the compassion days. Understanding without feeling can stay cold, or even be used against someone.
Together, they make it possible to know what's going on for a person, and to care. Fourth, a Stoic exercise in seeing the other side.

teach.h: ASK WHAT THEY THOUGHT WAS GOOD.
teach.b: Marcus Aurelius, in his Meditations, advises that when someone wrongs you, you first ask what they thought was good or bad when they did it. Once you see that, he writes, you'll feel pity rather than anger.
That's perspective-taking, used on purpose to soften the heart. Not to excuse the wrong. To see it from where they stood.

how: Some contemplative and therapeutic practices train perspective-taking directly, asking people to imagine another person's day or point of view, alongside practices that cultivate warmth toward them.

o: grasping someone's view, not only feeling their pain
picking a side in a fight between two friends
giving in to whoever you happen to be arguing with

games.q: seeing their side: tap the pairs.
p: working out what they think and want
being moved by what they feel
ask what they thought was good

s: understanding someone's view and feeling their feelings are the same thing
researchers separate the two, and a person can be strong in one and weaker in the other.
a person can read others well without being moved by them
a sharp negotiator can read a room without being moved by anyone in it.
Marcus Aurelius says seeing why someone did wrong means excusing it
he says it leads to pity rather than anger, not that the wrong stops being wrong.

games.q: a coworker snaps at you in a meeting. you want to respond well. what comes first?
o: snap back so it doesn't happen again.
ask what they were worried about, what they thought was at stake.
absorb their stress until you feel as bad as they do.
games.why: seeing their side first gives the feeling something to work with, without drowning in it.

practice: Choose someone who's been hard to understand lately and walk through a few hours of their day as if from inside it: where they wake up, the first worry, what's waiting at work or at home.
Then gently notice whether anything stirs toward them, warmth, sadness, patience, and let the seeing and the feeling each have a turn without forcing either.

wordCard.voice: Seeing their side. Understanding someone's view is different from feeling their feelings, and caring well needs both. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: their side. Seeing it clearly doesn't mean agreeing with it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Kanske, Singer and colleagues, research on empathy and theory of mind as separable routes to understanding others
